unit.title: Brand growth: availability and assets
unit.description: Brand equity, awareness, salience, mental and physical availability, distinctive assets, category entry points, brand versus performance

cards.definition: Evidence-based view of growth: brands grow mainly by winning more buyers, most of them light buyers, through mental availability (coming to mind) and physical availability (being easy to buy).
cards.example: A soda brand grows by being in more fridges and more minds, not by making its fans drink twice as much.

cards.term: The long and the short of it
cards.definition: Binet and Field analysis of effectiveness cases: brand building drives long-term growth, activation drives short-term sales. A balance close to 60 percent brand and 40 percent activation is often cited as a starting point; it varies by category.
cards.example: A B2B brand spending everything on search ads captures demand but stops creating it.

cards.definition: Using the same assets, tone and message for years, so memory structures build up. Marketers get bored of their campaigns long before customers notice them.
cards.example: A brand changing logo, colours and slogan every year has to start building recognition again each time.

exercises.prompt: According to Byron Sharp, how do brands mainly grow?
choices: By winning more buyers, especially light buyers
By making their loyal fans buy much more often
By targeting only a tiny niche of heavy users
By lowering their prices every quarter
exercises.explain: Penetration drives growth: big brands have many more buyers, most of whom buy rarely. Loyalty follows size.

choices: The chance your brand comes to mind in a buying situation
The number of shops that stock your products
The hours your customer service is open
The size of your email list
exercises.explain: Mental availability is built by distinctive assets and links to category entry points. Physical availability is the shop side.

exercises.prompt: What are the purple of Milka, the Intel jingle and the Michelin man?
choices: Distinctive brand assets
Category entry points
Brand equity measures
Price anchors
exercises.explain: Distinctive assets let people recognize the brand without its name. They take years of consistent use to build.

exercises.prompt: What are situations like I need a quick lunch or a gift for my host?
choices: Category entry points
Distinctive brand assets
Lead magnets
Brand guidelines
exercises.explain: CEPs are the cues that make buyers think of a category. Brands win by being linked to many of them.

exercises.prompt: Brand awareness and brand salience differ. What does salience add?
choices: Coming to mind at the moment of buying
Being recognized when the logo is shown
Having the highest price in the market
Being liked by people who never buy
exercises.explain: Recognition is awareness; salience is being thought of when it matters. A known brand can still be forgotten at the shelf.

exercises.prompt: A B2B company that spends all its budget on search ads only captures existing demand; it does not create new demand.
exercises.explain: True. Search captures people already looking. Brand building makes more people look for you later.

exercises.prompt: Binet and Field suggest which split as a frequent starting point between brand and activation?
choices: About 60 percent brand, 40 percent activation
About 10 percent brand, 90 percent activation
Exactly 50 percent brand, 50 percent activation
All on brand and nothing on activation
exercises.explain: The ratio varies by category and stage (more activation for new e-commerce, more brand for mature categories), but ignoring brand hurts long-term growth.

exercises.prompt: Your team is bored of the campaign after one year. What should you usually do?
choices: Keep the platform: customers have barely noticed it
Change the logo and the slogan right away
Stop all brand ads for a while
Run a totally new concept every month
exercises.explain: Consistency builds memory. Refresh executions, keep the assets and the core idea.

exercises.prompt: What does share of search compare?
choices: Your brand searches with the brand searches of your category
Your ad spend with the ad spend of rivals
Your SEO traffic with your paid traffic
Your followers with the followers of rivals
exercises.explain: Share of search is a cheap proxy of mental availability and often leads market share.

exercises.prompt: Which is a sign of strong brand equity?
choices: Customers pay more for your brand than for an equal product
Your logo was designed by a famous agency
Your company has existed for 100 years
You run more ads than all your competitors
exercises.explain: Brand equity is the value the name adds: price premium, preference, loyalty. A generic product with the same features sells for less.
